blocks.content: Round Robin is the scheduling algorithm built specifically for time sharing and interactive systems, where fairness and responsiveness matter more than squeezing out the lowest possible average waiting time. Every process gets a fair, bounded turn on the processor, and no single process, however long its total work, can ever make another process wait forever.

This chapter explains the Round Robin algorithm precisely, works through a full numeric example with a Gantt chart trace and a completion, turnaround and waiting time table, digs into why the size of the time quantum is the single most important decision behind Round Robin, gives a practical rule of thumb for picking one, explains exactly why the algorithm guarantees good response time, compares it against FCFS and SJF, and closes with common mistakes and the interview angle.
1. What Round Robin Is

Round Robin keeps every process in the ready queue and gives each one a fixed, small unit of CPU time called a time quantum, also called a time slice. A process runs only for the length of that quantum. If it finishes its burst before the quantum runs out, it leaves the CPU on its own, exactly like any other algorithm. But if the quantum expires while the process still has work left to do, the scheduler forcibly preempts it, the process is placed at the back of the ready queue, and the CPU immediately moves on to whichever process is now at the front. This cycle repeats continuously, every process taking its turn, being sent to the back if it is not finished, and waiting for the queue to rotate all the way around again before it gets another quantum. That continuous rotation through the queue is exactly where the name round robin comes from.

blocks.title: In one sentence
blocks.content: Round Robin gives every process a fixed time quantum, preempts it to the back of the ready queue if it is not done when the quantum expires, and keeps rotating through the queue until every process has completed.

["Pick the process at the front of the ready queue.","Let it run for at most one time quantum.","If it finishes within the quantum, remove it from the system and move on to the next process.","If the quantum expires and the process still has work left, preempt it and place it at the back of the ready queue.","Move to the new front of the queue and repeat."]
items: Pick the process at the front of the ready queue.
Let it run for at most one time quantum.
If it finishes within the quantum, remove it from the system and move on to the next process.
If the quantum expires and the process still has work left, preempt it and place it at the back of the ready queue.
Move to the new front of the queue and repeat.

blocks.title: A way to picture it
blocks.content: Round Robin runs like a strict meeting moderator. Each speaker gets exactly two minutes at the microphone. When the two minutes are up, the microphone moves to the next speaker no matter what, and if the first speaker still had more to say, they rejoin the back of the line and wait their turn to speak again. Nobody gets to hold the microphone forever, and everybody is guaranteed to get it back eventually.
2. A Fully Worked Example
Take four processes, P1, P2, P3 and P4, all arriving at time zero, with a time quantum of four units.

The ready queue starts as P1, P2, P3, P4, in that order. The scheduler runs P1 for one quantum of four units, leaving six units remaining, then sends it to the back of the queue. It then runs P2 for four units, leaving one unit remaining, and sends it to the back too. The same happens to P3 and P4, each getting exactly one quantum before being preempted and rejoining at the back with whatever work is still left. Once the first full rotation of the queue is done, the scheduler starts a second rotation, this time picking up P1 again with its six remaining units, and so on, until every process has finally used up its full burst time.

blocks.content: Completion time is simply the clock time at which the trace above shows each process finishing its final slice. Turnaround time is completion time minus arrival time, and since every process here arrived at time zero, turnaround time equals completion time. Waiting time is turnaround time minus burst time, the portion of the total time a process spent sitting in the ready queue rather than actually running on the CPU.

Average waiting time works out to nineteen plus sixteen plus seventeen plus twenty one, divided by four, which is eighteen point two five units. Average turnaround time works out to twenty nine plus twenty one plus twenty five plus twenty seven, divided by four, which is twenty five point five units. Notice that no process ever waits an unbounded amount of time between turns. Every process is guaranteed to be revisited once every full rotation of the queue, and that predictable rhythm is the entire point of Round Robin.
3. Choosing the Time Quantum: Two Ways To Get It Wrong
blocks.text: 3. Choosing the Time Quantum: Two Ways To Get It Wrong

blocks.content: Everything about how well Round Robin performs comes down to one number, the size of the time quantum. Pick it badly in either direction and the algorithm stops behaving like Round Robin at all.
Quantum too large

If the quantum is set far larger than most processes actually need, then most processes finish their entire burst comfortably inside a single quantum. They never actually get preempted, because they are done long before the quantum would have expired. In that situation Round Robin quietly degrades into something that behaves just like FCFS, since processes effectively run to completion in arrival order anyway. All the responsiveness that Round Robin is supposed to offer disappears, because a short interactive process can still end up waiting behind one long process that happens to be ahead of it in the queue, exactly the convoy style problem Round Robin was designed to avoid.
Quantum too small

If the quantum is set too small, the opposite problem appears. A context switch happens every single time the quantum expires, and a context switch is not free, it costs real time to save the state of the process being paused and load the state of the next one. When the quantum is tiny, the scheduler ends up performing a context switch almost as often as it performs useful work, so a disproportionate share of CPU time goes into switching between processes rather than actually running them. Taken to an extreme, a quantum small enough can make the system spend more total time context switching than computing, leaving actual throughput worse than a much simpler algorithm like FCFS would have delivered on the very same workload.

A quantum that is too large makes Round Robin behave like FCFS. A quantum that is too small makes the system spend more time switching between processes than running them. The right quantum sits somewhere between these two extremes.
4. A Practical Rule of Thumb

There is no single correct quantum size for every workload, since it depends entirely on how long typical CPU bursts are on that particular system. What operating systems textbooks and real schedulers commonly rely on instead is a rule of thumb tied to the actual distribution of burst lengths rather than a fixed constant.

A good time quantum is chosen so that roughly eighty percent of CPU bursts are shorter than the quantum. That way most processes finish within a single slice and behave responsively, while the quantum still stays small enough to keep context switching overhead under control.

This rule balances the two failure extremes directly. A quantum large enough that eighty percent of bursts fit inside it keeps most processes from suffering repeated preemptions, which limits context switch overhead. At the same time, since the quantum is sized against the actual burst distribution rather than picked arbitrarily large, the remaining longer processes still get preempted regularly enough that short, interactive processes never have to wait long for their turn.
5. Why Round Robin Guarantees Good Response Time
blocks.text: 5. Why Round Robin Guarantees Good Response Time

blocks.content: The defining strength of Round Robin is that no process can ever be starved of its first turn on the CPU. Since the ready queue rotates through every process exactly once per cycle, and each process ahead of a given process can consume at most one quantum before being sent to the back, the longest a process can possibly wait before receiving its very first burst of CPU time is bounded. If there are n processes in the ready queue, a process at the very back has at most n minus one processes ahead of it, each of which uses at most one quantum, so the worst case wait before that process first runs is at most quantum multiplied by n minus one.

blocks.title: Tying it back to the worked example
blocks.content: In the trace from section two, P4 was fourth in line behind three other processes with a quantum of four. True to the formula, P4 received its very first burst of CPU time at time twelve, exactly three multiplied by four, matching n minus one multiplied by the quantum with n equal to four processes.

This bounded wait for a first response is exactly what makes Round Robin so well suited to interactive, time sharing systems. A user typing at a terminal or clicking in an application does not need their process to finish quickly, they need it to start responding quickly, and Round Robin is one of the few classic algorithms that can make that guarantee mathematically, not just in practice.
6. Round Robin Compared With FCFS and SJF
blocks.text: 6. Round Robin Compared With FCFS and SJF

blocks.content: Placing Round Robin next to the two algorithms covered earlier makes its tradeoffs clear. FCFS and SJF both aim to finish processes efficiently overall, while Round Robin aims to keep every process responsive along the way, even at some cost to average waiting time.

The pattern is consistent across the whole table. FCFS optimizes for nothing but arrival order, SJF optimizes for average waiting time at the cost of fairness to long processes, and Round Robin deliberately trades away some average waiting time in exchange for a guarantee that no process, long or short, is ever left waiting indefinitely for its turn.
7. Common Mistakes
Forgetting that a preempted process goes to the back of the queue
blocks.text: Forgetting that a preempted process goes to the back of the queue

blocks.content: When a quantum expires and a process still has work left, it does not stay at the front of the ready queue and it is never given priority over processes that have not run yet. It goes strictly to the back, behind every process that is already waiting, and only reaches the front again once the queue has rotated all the way around. Placing a preempted process back at the front by mistake turns Round Robin into something closer to a single process hogging the CPU with brief interruptions, which defeats the entire purpose of the algorithm.
Picking a quantum size without considering the tradeoff
blocks.text: Picking a quantum size without considering the tradeoff

blocks.content: Choosing a quantum arbitrarily, without thinking about the actual distribution of burst lengths on the system, is a common shortcut that causes real problems. A quantum picked too casually can easily land on one of the two failure extremes, either drifting toward FCFS behavior because it is too generous, or drowning the system in context switch overhead because it is too stingy. The quantum should always be chosen with the tradeoff in mind, ideally using a guideline like the eighty percent rule rather than a round number picked for convenience.
8. The Interview Angle

Round Robin is a favorite interview topic because tracing a basic example, watching processes rotate through the queue and computing completion, turnaround and waiting times, only tests the mechanics. The real follow up question almost always concerns the time quantum: what happens if it is set larger, what happens if it is set smaller, and how would you choose a sensible value for a real system. A strong answer walks through both failure extremes confidently, ties response time back to the bound of quantum multiplied by the number of processes, and mentions the eighty percent rule of thumb as a concrete, defensible way to pick a quantum rather than guessing at a number.

blocks.title: Quick recap to keep ready
blocks.content: Round Robin preempts a process to the back of the queue when its time quantum expires. Too large a quantum drifts toward FCFS behavior. Too small a quantum wastes time on context switching. A good quantum is sized so roughly eighty percent of bursts finish within it. Worst case wait for a first response is bounded by quantum multiplied by the number of processes ahead in the queue.
